And so I think one thing that is an exciting opportunity for OpenRadar, generally speaking, is like, you know, um, helping to Helping developers understand what these sort of subtle differences are so that they can make the most informed decisions about what models ultimately they select. And then also you can imagine the flip side of that, which is, you have all these developers using these models. And so those developers are great people to ask about what are the interesting textual differences between these models that are more than just tweet length. Like, this model’s good, this model’s bad, more than just that level of insight. And I think this is like getting to the wine sommelier version or form of understanding the models and their sort of relative strengths and weaknesses, I think would be quite exciting.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Okay, so based on your experience, the OpenRadar view that there will be a diversity of models in the future and they’re optimized for different tasks and—

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: I agree with that.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Exactly. That’s just your guys’ experience based on—

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Yeah, we are focusing On different things. We care a lot more about personal and professional agents, my observation, than the other major labs, which is good. There should be differentiation in the economy. This is the point of capitalism to some extent.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: So you’re going to say something?

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: No, I just really agree with that point. I mean, I think that part of what I love about you guys working on OpenRouter and being able to scale it is just the more infrastructure that can get developed, that supports a diversity of players in the ecosystem, I think is good overall. I also, for the same reason, am quite a fan of some of the recent NVIDIA moves to support the open source ecosystem. I don’t know, but this just kind of goes with our whole theory and philosophy about, like, what does a good future look like?

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Mm-hmm.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: We think that a good future is one where you achieve a, like, you basically get prosperity by empowering people. That’s kind of the personal superintelligence thing that we’re doing, but there’s the whole business version.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: But for a lot of the important safety topics, like, our view is that the way to get there is having a diversity and having checks and balances by kind of having a lot of different things out there and accessible to people, not like just having a couple of good models that are only in a couple companies’ hands. I think that that would be— from my perspective, I think that is probably a riskier configuration for the future than lots of people having access to different things.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Do you guys have a theory as to why that is? Where I feel like maybe people predicted more of a winner-takes-all dynamic in AI, or one person clearly— like, a story that people told back in 2023 is that one AI lab will start to develop an advantage, and that will allow them to get recursive self-improvement going, And then they’ll just pull further and further away from everyone else. Whereas it has remained extremely competitive where there’s kind of multiple people at the frontier. You guys with Wonder today are coming along with your frontier-class model. Open source models have done an impressive job of keeping up, all told. And so we had this story a few years ago that someone was just going to run away with the prize. Why hasn’t that happened?

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: I think there’s a lot of underlying reasons and mechanics that drive this. One certainly is just execution. I think for any given frontier lab, there are periods of strong execution and weak execution. And I think that is true across all the labs. And so that sort of starts to average itself out over time. I think another—

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: Very diplomatic.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Sorry.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Is it that some of the Players in the lead screwed up?

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Well, I think if all players, when they were in the lead, executed perfectly, they would probably be able to stay in the lead. So I think that’s one factor. I think the power and strength of distillation is certainly another factor that’s certainly benefiting the open source ecosystem quite a bit. And I think this is just like a—

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: There’s an anti-hegemonic force in the phenomenon of distilling a model.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Yeah. And this is just a quality of the technology. It’s not like anyone planned for distillation to work super duper well, but it just turns out that you can get a lot of capabilities naturally through some form of distillation. And this is, broadly speaking, distillation is quite a good force for the entire ecosystem because it means that you can pack very strong intelligence capabilities into smaller and smaller models, which enables us to serve them at much wider scale. And that’s certainly one of the very exciting stories is just like really small models today are like, you know, much more powerful than the biggest models a year ago or 2 years ago. And then I think the last is that there’s just sort of this— I think there’s like, I actually think a lot of people in the ecosystem want this future where it is not just this like, you know, definitely. One final company in all of capitalism kind of kind of end outcome. Like, I think this is one of the reasons—

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Not just individuals, but companies putting dollars against things.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Yeah. And I think, like, you know, this is actually one of the reasons why a lot of people were excited to join Meta and Meta Superintelligence Labs in the first place, was that they were just sort of like, you know, I want to work at a place that is focused on giving this technology to billions of people. That is, like, not the stated goal necessarily of all the other frontier labs. And so, I think there’s, like, a lot of sort of just, like, natural forces where many people in the industry are sort of, like, grappling with, okay, what is the actual world state that I want to live in in the future? And there’s lots of sort of, like, decisions that people make at all levels in terms of where they work or who they do business with or what business deals they do that sort of, like, drive towards a more equalized outcome.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: You get into the Some of the MSL startup, which I also wanted to ask about, which is it just seems fundamentally very hard still to— again, we talked about what goes into developing a frontier model, but also from a standing start, like when was the standing start for MSL?

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: Well, we launched Llama 4 on April 4th, I think it was, 2025. Right. And then I think, what was it, April 20th or 21st was, I think, when I was like, hey, when I started calling people for advice on what to do.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: So, I remember I was in a staff meeting and I got, like, the WhatsApp notification, like, have time for a call? I was like, huh, interesting.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Okay, so MSL is a little over 2 years old.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: No, no, no, 1 year. 1 year.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Is it ‘25? Oh, it’s ‘26. Oh, sorry, I’m living in the future.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: Yeah, you are in the future.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: MSL is a little over 1 year old. Um, yeah, what are your reflections a little over a year in on what was load-bearing, as the IAs would say, in how it came together?

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: Well, I mean, I think that there was this whole thing early on which is just like, first we had to pull together this core group. Right? So, um, so Nat and Alex and I, we were like talking a bit up front, um, and, you know, at first we were, you know, brainstorming. Yeah, like I was talking to Nat about, could we— is there a way that we can like structure this so that way it’s like a win for Alex’s shareholders and like we can like get him over here? And then, so then we were talking about, uh, like what would the plan be? And, and then basically I was just, I was in this mode where I was just like asking a lot of different people what we should do. And like every time that, that we would talk, I’d come away with like 3 more things of like, oh yeah, this is what we should do. It’s like very like high signal, very like a lot of strategic clarity. And so we were brainstorming and working on this for a bit. And then Nat and Daniel joined and we pulled together a few of the the initial researchers.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: But like, in the beginning, it was sort of like the Supernova thing where we just kind of like jammed a bunch of people together. And I don’t know, it was like, I don’t think either of us slept that much for the first couple of months.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: I like, don’t even, I kind of have this mental block almost where I like, I kind of almost cleared my calendar for like a month or 2 and was just meeting researchers and talking to them. And I remember even before we announced the deal where you were going to come over, we were basically like, you were recruiting people and people were like, what is going on? Like, it’s like, what is this?

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: But, um, but then there was the whole question, which was a really hands-on data labeler.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: But, but that was, that was this whole question too, where it’s like, all right, well, like, okay, so if we’re not happy with the trajectory of the current program, Like, who were the right set of people to lead the program going forward? And Alex and I had spent a bunch of time talking over the years. I mean, maybe like, whatever, once every few months or something we’d talk. And I was always just very impressed by how he thought about things strategically. And I kind of had this view of like, all right, yeah, currently he’s doing this very operational data business. But it always felt to me like he was the sharpest entrepreneur of his generation, of the ones who I had had a chance to meet. And like, it always just struck me, it’s like, all right, like, this is a guy who, yeah, he’s like running this like kind of very grindy operational business, but like—

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Lovely business still, by the way.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: What’s up? We’re big investors. It’s not a— it’s a— there’s more Commentary on the difficulty of running the business.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: When you run the 8th wonder of the world, Alex, a lot of businesses look like a grindy operational business.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: It’s just like my view of things. It’s like grindy, grindy. No, no, no. But no, so it’s, so I just kind of had this view. I’m like, all right, like, even though this is sort of I think maybe when we got started, a lot of people were like, okay, like, how is this going to work? It’s like the kind of like the social media guy is working with the like data guy.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Like, is that like, are we going to build a frontier lab here or what?

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: But, but I mean, but my, but I mean, my like really strong conviction, because I talked to like all the leaders of all the labs, like all the heads of research, like all this stuff. And like, I was like, no, Alex is the guy. Like, he’s the fucking guy. And like, and we’re going to, and basically, like, we’re going to basically be able to, to, to go pull together a team and recruit the people that we need to go do this. And like, we need this kind of very, this kind of like strategic clarity that he has around the different ways that we want to approach this, the kind of extreme focus on talent density, on kind of like the clarity of communicating the different vision, which we kind of fashioned together over this period. And a bunch of things that I think were kind of extreme but have basically worked, like having this, this like very flat culture was something that you were kind of really obsessed with, right? It’s, I mean, you have like, was it almost 200 direct reports? That’s like, we have, it’s not, it doesn’t, it’s not quite that extreme in practice.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: I think that there’s like, like team leads and all, and all this stuff.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: My muse helps me manage that.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: Yeah, well, that’s— But like, but there were these series of things that I think quite early we, you kind of articulated, and I was like, okay, this is like kind of extreme, but it seems like directionally right, and like we should go do this. And, you know, I went and like talked to other people who were more like the people you’d conventionally think of, and it’s like, it was just very much like, I don’t know what you’d expect expect a big company to operate. And I was like, no, we want to do something that’s—

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: As you describe this, I’ll note 4 things that I think even other opinionated, effective founder CEOs would not have done. One, you just called the recent prior effort by a bunch of people at the company a failure and not good enough. I mean, you were more diplomatic than that, but the act of standing up off the trajectory— Yeah, but the act of standing up So, you know, people can read between the lines.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: So sometimes, yeah, sometimes you have to reboot a team.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: That’s one. Thing 2 is you are willing to pay ungodly amounts of money for effectively talent. Like, you’re paying a lot of money to bring Alex and some other people, but, you know, a lot of money for Alex in particular over. Thing 3—

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: And 49% of this very good grindy business. Yeah, exactly.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: But let’s keep the story straight. So there’s that. Thing 3 is, I’ll note, Alex had never trained a frontier model before. And so you were taking some amount of a bet on Alex’s potential to do something where he had done stuff in AI, but no offense, he just had not done the specific thing that you were being hired to do. And then 4th, you were saying you cleared your calendar and just only did this for 2 months. I think a lot of CEOs would’ve had the business review and would have had the board thing and they would have had the customer stuff and things like that. Those 4 seem to me pretty interesting where I think a lot of CEOs would not have done those.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: Yeah, that’s interesting.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: I definitely think— I mean, one thing you may not appreciate this about yourself, but I think one thing that is quite special about Marc is the degree to which, like, once he concludes that something is the right thing or something makes sense, he just like fully shifts everything to be consistent with that belief set. And it is quite like, to your point, I think like the inertia of most, even very successful founders who like are opinionated and edgy or whatnot, would just be to like, oh, I still have like my whole calendar. And like, so I’ll just like talk about doing this thing and hope that somebody does it kind of situation. Whereas I think, No, I think when Marc concludes that something is the thing he has to do or makes a lot of sense, then he really does, like, he has, like, maybe very high learning rate in that sense. Like, he’s very willing to, like, pivot entire things to be consistent with it. And I think that, like, you know, one very underappreciated thing is the degree to which so much of the company had to pivot to support MSL as well.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Like, I think that while it was a kind of like this more startup-y effort within a larger company, you know, the needs of MSL were still quite large. Like, we needed a huge amount of help on infrastructure. We needed these large-scale data centers to be built. We needed like lots of support from many other parts of the company. And especially as Muse has been successful, we’ve also needed lots of—

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Deep collaboration with the rest of the company. And this is one thing that I think kind of only is possible because Mark is the founder CEO, and he can ensure that we have kind of like a global optimization towards this sort of like AI maximalist version of Meta versus the natural inertia of an organization towards just local optimization ad infinitum.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: But it’s also a lot of how we work together is it’s important to me to be in the details of this work so that we can get everything around the company to go do what we need to do. Right. And so it’s like, I mean, yeah, I’ll have opinions about this stuff, but I’m not like, I’m not the lead researcher.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Right.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: It’s like, it’s, you know, it’s, but I think that’s kind of a lot of, I think how we work together well is that, yeah, it’s, I mean, we’re, we’re kind of like, quite in the details of all of this stuff, but running the lab is a big thing. Running the rest of the company in order to support this is like the effort is a big thing. You almost like, you can’t really get this done, I think, without both of those pieces.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: And one thing that I think was quite important about when we set the whole thing up is Meta, the company, invested a huge amount to stand up MSL, and then we very clearly told everyone like, hey, there’s no deadlines. We are going to take things at the right pace, which I think on the one hand could be like, you know, absolutely terrifying. It’s like you’ve just like stood up this extremely expensive unit and you’re telling everyone like, hey—

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Yeah, and you’re worried inside a larger company that like, okay, 7 years from now maybe something will ship, right?

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Yeah, totally. And so, but I think that like, first, I think one of the cool things about, you know, focusing on talent density and hiring all these very brilliant people who have done so much already, that’s very impressive, is, you know, everybody had like a lot of motivation to ship and everybody wanted to sort of like leave their mark, so to speak, on the field. And so everybody was like heavily, highly self-motivated to move as quickly as possible. And one of the things that’s been funny and I’ve had to continue reminding the team of is like, you know, it is a team of a lot of insecure overachievers. So like at any one point, if I ask them like, hey, how good do you think— where do you think we’ll be in 3 months? I always get the most like—

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Everyone always says it’s awful. It’s awful.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: We’re screwed.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: These like very pessimistic answers. And then I record it and I like 3 months later I’m like, hey, you know, we just shipped this model. Let me just show you what all of you said, where all of you said we would be in 3 3 months ago. And, uh, and this is—

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: And has that caused them to get any more optimistic or no?

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: No, they’re still—

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: they’re very self-critical. I think it’s, it’s not, it’s not that they’re pessimistic about— I think that the average person seems quite optimistic about MSL and very self-critical about their own project. Yeah. Which I think is actually quite a healthy, a healthy dynamic.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Um, but, but the trend continues. Like, I think, I think, and, and this is, I mean, in many ways Muse Wonder is like this incredible milestone for everyone because it is a—

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: The team was very, very critical.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: That was working on it along the way.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: When did you guys know that Muse Wanderer was good?

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Um, that’s a good question. I think that we, uh, so there’s all these intermediate drawings.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: You’re peeking in the oven and it’s like, I don’t know, it seems kind of gooey still.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: And yeah, yeah, going back to it, I mean, there are all these intermediate intermediate signals that you can get along the way that things are good or bad.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: And what are the intermediate signals?

items.text: So in pre-training, you have a lot of perplexity-based evaluation. So you have a different regime of evals that can help you in pre-training. And then you have the more traditional benchmarks that can help you towards RL. But no, I mean, this model, kind of as you mentioned, has been cooking for quite a while. And You know, a lot of— I think one of the funniest things about AI research is that, you know, there’s a lot of times where people just sort of like are kind of squinting at a bunch of dots and being like, yeah, looks like it’s good, or, uh, looks a little bit off. Like, one of the funniest things is the people have protractors, like analog protractors that they put against you know, a set of lines on their monitor to like measure an angle. And then they, um, so he’s not come for this job yet. So I think there’s, I think there’s like a huge amount of like, uh, like it’s very, um, there’s more vibes, um, driving like, okay.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: But when did we have this conversation where, when did you know it was good?

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: Um, well, we had this debate after it was done pre-training where it was okay. How long will it take in RL before it is better than Muse Spark? And I remember the folks on the pre-training team were just trying to set expectations. They’re like, look, sometimes this takes a while. And then it was immediately. And so we were like, okay, I think we’re on a good path. That to me was sort of—

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: I think when when people got— yeah.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: We’ve been excited. I think we’ve been pretty excited about it for a few months now. Yeah.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: But there’s a lot to do there. But going back to the beginning, I think one of the things that was very interesting and challenging in standing the thing up was like, you really just wanted this like very high talent density effort. And we were just kind of pulling some of the best people from Meta in and recruiting a lot of the best people. And I mean, you were asking, it’s like, all right, well, like, okay, for people who, like, if you were asking before, it’s like, well, Alex hadn’t necessarily trained models like this. But to me, one of the big things was like all of the best people were very excited to work with him. And I think like, it’s, I mean, you, I’m sure see this in all of, in a lot of the things that you do, which is like, you know, it’s like you, most people are not kind of one-dimensional, right? Yeah, maybe you do a specific thing, but your ability to grow and expand is kind of largely based on how effectively can you just do people who are excellent in different domains want to come work with you on different things.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Yeah, and the great people have followership.

items.speaker: Alexandr Wang
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: And so I think that there was a little bit of that, but also just It’s even for the people that don’t know you yet, or like, or aren’t, you know, don’t know what you’re about. Like, are you like an impressive person and a compelling person that people want to come work with? Do people feel comfortable that you’re going to create this environment? And I think you were like very thoughtful about this early on. We were kind of— Some of the stuff I think you kind of had fully formed as beliefs of how you thought we should do this. But I also remember when we were having the initial recruiting conversations, we were sort of in real time shaping— it’s like, okay, well, this construct that we’re talking about with this person isn’t quite going to work, but like, they seem good, and like, they have this thought. And it was just like, like, really kind of coalescing this vision about what the shape of it should be in real time. I mean, I don’t know, I mean, I’m sure you remember that. this, where it was like there were some of the initial concepts of like, I mean, I think probably the most extreme thing was I think you had the concept of the talent density and all and that kind of piece.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: But I think we weren’t sure upfront that it was going to have to be a full reboot, right? It’s like that basically started when we were out talking to a lot of the kind of best people. And we realized that, hey, like, in order to make this as attractive as possible, it should feel like, okay, we’re starting this thing again from scratch. And yeah, we’ll pull in a lot of the great people from the Llama effort and FAIR and all of that too. But that was a very intentional thing that we basically figured out and that you figured out as we were out talking to the initial set of people of like what was going to make this compelling. And it ended up being really smart and like making a huge difference in the culture of the lab and how it got and how it got started. But I don’t know, it’s like being able to be that dynamic about figuring out, like, what does the shape of this need to be? It’s not like that. I think that’s a very uncommon trait. It’s a very entrepreneurial trait, right? So, when I was thinking about, like, all right, like, this field is going to keep on evolving, right?

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: So, what is the thing that’s going to be important for someone who’s going to run a lab well? It’s not like, are they an expert in whatever the latest modality is of, like, or kind of of training technique for a lab. It’s, is the person a clear thinker and able to kind of dynamically update and move in, like, as kind of an entrepreneur would? I think this is just like an inherently very entrepreneurial space.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Has this experience changed your view on the value of going external, where both your reboot, a bunch of the people you brought in were external, like Alex and Nat and Daniel and folks. But then also you’re describing deciding whether you needed a reboot based on going to the outside intelligence of the aggregate views of the researchers in the industry and getting a sense for the— But just Do you feel like you’ll carry forward that approach for future unrelated projects? Because obviously the risk of a large company is that everyone’s like, oh, we got a great approach. Yeah, let me show you our 100-page document on it.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: I mean, obviously you can’t— a lot of what we had to do here was rotate a lot of the rest of the company. And like for things like the infrastructure team that now, you know, it’s like building these huge clusters to support this. I mean, that’s obviously a huge thing. So huge parts of the company kind of had to pivot to do this. And obviously you can’t do too many of those at the same time, right? Only one thing can be the top priority.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: But I think on balance, it has made me somewhat more optimistic. I mean, we brought in this guy Kunal Shah, who, you know, it’s like, I think he’s like one of the top entrepreneurs in India, building this great company CRED, and And now he’s running WhatsApp, which I always thought should do more in commerce, and we were sort of underserved there, and India is the biggest country that we’re in. But, I mean, that’s— it’s a bit of a different situation, because we’re not, like, pivoting the whole company towards WhatsApp. We just wanted to bring more entrepreneurial energy there. This was, like, a level 10 out of 10 difficulty thing. I don’t want to talk about it in the past tense, as if it’s done, because it’s still a level 10 out of 10 difficulty thing.

items.speaker: John Collison
items.text: Yeah, yeah, sure.

items.speaker: Mark Zuckerberg
items.text: But I think the number of pieces that kind of had to work, it was quite all-encompassing. And I think that it’s both difficult for the people doing it, but I do think that that also puts some level of strain on the rest of the company, on the financial model of the company. I think like you— so I wouldn’t want to conflate those 2 pieces. Right? It’s like I think there’s yeah, it’s good to have new blood, and it’s good to have people who understand the context. And you know, you were talking about people who’ve been around Meta for a while and understand the ups and downs.
